query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A one-step, controlled thermal shock treatment can induce the formation of a self-adaptive, nanostructured oxide/HEA composite tribolayer on the HEA surface that simultaneously reduces the friction coefficient and wear rate over a service-temperature range from ambient to ~700°C.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy (HEA) in its untreated, bulk, single-phase state (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo or similar) used in self-lubricating moving component applications.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal shock treatment (with a rapid temperature ramp to a high set-point, a defined dwell time, and controlled ambient atmosphere) to induce surface oxidation and rapid nanostructural evolution.
generation.conditions: The treatment is designed to be effective under sliding tribological conditions across a broad temperature range (ambient up to approximately 700°C) and under mechanical loads typical for self-lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: A self-adaptive, nanostructured composite tribolayer consisting of a dense, protective oxide phase (e.g., ZrTiO4-like) intimately integrated with refined HEA nanostructures or 2D HEA nanoflakes.
generation.mechanism: The rapid thermal shock rapidly oxidizes the near-surface region, forming a stable protective oxide layer while simultaneously inducing dynamic amorphization and grain refinement. This composite layer adapts its structure during sliding to reduce shear strength (thus lowering friction) and protect against material loss (thus reducing wear) across varying temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated HEA, the treated alloy will exhibit a substantially lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate (e.g., friction reduction by approximately 50% and wear rate reduction by roughly an order of magnitude) across the full service temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA surfaces that lack the engineered nanostructured oxide layer and exhibit separate or limited improvements in friction or wear under narrow temperature windows.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective provided that the thermal shock parameters (peak temperature, dwell time, and ambient oxygen level) are optimized; deviations that lead to over-oxidation or insufficient oxide layer formation may compromise the performance. Extreme mechanical stresses or environments with reactive species beyond design assumptions may also limit effectiveness.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in friction and wear (i.e., percentage reduction and order-of-magnitude changes) depend sensitively on the thermal shock parameters, and further optimization may be required. The mechanism’s effectiveness across the entire temperature range is inferred from analogous studies but remains to be fully validated under all operating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA samples. Subject one group to the controlled thermal shock treatment under the prescribed parameters while retaining the other group as untreated controls. Conduct systematic ball-on-disk tribological tests across a series of temperatures spanning ambient up to ~700°C under identical mechanical loads. Use surface characterization techniques (e.g., XRD, SEM) to verify the formation of the composite tribolayer post-treatment.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during steady-state sliding
Wear rate (volume loss per applied load and sliding distance)
Surface microstructure and phase analysis (to confirm formation of the nanostructured oxide/HEA composite layer)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal-shock-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the friction coefficient and wear rate (relative to the untreated controls) across the entire temperature range, or if the expected composite tribolayer is not observed through surface characterization, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

decision.trend: Early studies showed that tailoring the near‐surface microstructure of HEAs (e.g., via dynamic amorphization leading to ultra-nanocrystalline layers) and introducing reinforcing phases (like WC via laser cladding) could individually lower friction or wear. Subsequent work then demonstrated that deliberate thermal treatments can induce the formation of dense, protective oxide layers (as seen in thermal shock experiments) and that 2D HEA nanoflakes can provide self-lubricating, tribocatalytic surfaces. The evolution has been from bulk or microstructure adjustments that improved one metric at a time to surface modifications that promote self-adaptive, multi-scale lubrication. However, these approaches have not yet been unified into a single intervention that guarantees both low friction and low wear over a wide temperature span.
decision.unsolved: A critical gap remains in creating a singular, robust modification that reliably activates self-adaptive lubrication phenomena across the entire service-temperature range—from ambient to high (e.g., up to ~700°C) environments—without compromising the mechanical integrity or requiring multiple processing steps.
decision.lever: controlled thermal shock treatment to induce a self-adaptive, nanostructured oxide/HEA composite tribolayer
decision.why: This lever follows from the observed benefits of thermally induced passivation layers (as in PMC10456374) and the proven low friction behavior of self-lubricating 2D HEA nanoflakes (as in PMC12019924). By precisely tuning the thermal shock parameters (temperature ramp, dwell time, and ambient atmosphere), the intervention is expected to form a robust surface layer that dynamically adapts its structure—maintaining lubricity by offsetting wear at both cryogenic and high temperatures—thus addressing the dual challenge of friction and wear reduction in a single, unified step.
